achira.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a tourist bows too deep and asks, ever so formally, where the enormous bell hangs. Grandma Kane doesn't just point — she straightens up, sweeps her whole arm in a slow, ceremonial arc past the mossy steps and every lounging cat, all the way to the far tower, because when the distance is real and the company deserves manners, you don't jab a finger — you gesture, grandly, over there.
achira.reading_mnemonic: You already know あ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>あちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"ah-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, nothing hidden underneath.
achira.description: This is the polite, distance-marking form of "over there" — the one you use with strangers, customers, or anyone above you in status, not the clipped, casual version you'd use with close friends. Point far away formally, not with a jabbed finger.

anata.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till breaks and starts beeping the same word at whoever steps up to pay — anata, anata — refusing to learn a single name. Customers give up introducing themselves and just answer to it, until the word stops being rude and becomes the only way anyone in that line ever gets addressed: you.
anata.reading_mnemonic: あなた is written exactly the way it sounds — plain kana, no kanji hiding a different reading — so the word you say is simply 「<reading>あなた</reading>」.
anata.description: In real conversation あなた is used sparingly — Japanese usually addresses people by name or title, and aiming あなた at a stranger or superior can sound distant or even confrontational; it is most naturally heard from a wife speaking to her husband.

anna.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, Sei points at the vending machine improbably perched at the summit, far beyond arm's reach, and mutters that only that kind of machine — the distant one neither of them chose — would end up all the way up there.
anna.reading_mnemonic: This is another kana-only word, so <reading>あんな</reading> is simply read as written, with no separate derivation needed.

ano.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a goat sits down across the path and will not budge until you say what you are climbing toward. You point at the vending machine improbably parked at the summit, a speck against the sky, and groan ah, no, not that far. The goat only accepts things too distant to touch: that vending machine over there, that peak over there.
ano.reading_mnemonic: Nothing hidden in this one: it is written in kana exactly the way it is spoken, <reading>あの</reading>.
ano.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something far from both you and the listener, or at something you both already know about even when it is nowhere in sight. Stretched out on its own, with the first vowel held, it is also the ordinary hesitation noise, roughly English um, and carries no pointing sense at all.

are.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail you and a stranger both stop and squint at the vending machine glowing at the very summit, hopelessly far from either of you. All you can manage is a long flat ahh, and the stranger adds a defeated eh. Nobody is reaching it today. Not near you, not near them, just a speck up the slope — that over there.
are.reading_mnemonic: Kana only, said exactly as it is written: <reading>あれ</reading>, with nothing to decode.
are.description: Used for something far from both you and the person you are talking to, not merely far from you. It also does duty for a thing you both already know about but is not present — the that in that trip we took — which is why it turns up so often in conversation with no object in sight.

asoko.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a stray sock slips off the washing line and drifts downstream before anyone notices. By the time someone looks up, it's bobbing far off, snagged on a rock past the bend — not here, not nearby, just over there. That distant, can't-quite-reach spot is exactly what this word points at: over there.
asoko.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>あそこ</reading>, nothing more to decode.

boku.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a boy waist-deep in the current catches nothing all afternoon, and when a fish finally leaps straight into his rival's net instead of his own, he plants his rod in the mud and announces to the whole bank that he, personally, will be the one telling this story later — not his friend, not the fish, him. That flat, proud claim to being the one talking is the meaning you want: I, said the rough, boyish way a kid says it.
boku.reading_mnemonic: He slaps his soggy fishing log down on a rock and reads the cover aloud in a gruff voice, <reading>book</reading>, <reading>book</reading>, until it slurs into <reading>ぼく</reading> — the plain, boyish way to say I that he now uses for himself as often as for the log.
boku.description: Used mainly by men and boys, in casual to neutral speech; it reads as too soft or boyish for very formal contexts and is rarely used by adult women.

dare.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell rings itself in the dead of night. The cats scatter, the mossy steps creak, and no one is standing anywhere near the rope. Grandma Kane storms out onto the steps demanding an answer to the only question that matters: who.
dare.reading_mnemonic: Every night the bell rings and nobody's there, so Grandma Kane leans out over the mossy steps and bellows into the dark: who <reading>dares</reading> touch my bell? The cats scatter at the challenge in her voice, and that same dare is exactly the sound of <reading>だれ</reading> — the question of who it could possibly be.

dochira.meaning_mnemonic: You've dragged yourself up the mountain trail to the one improbable vending machine at the top, expecting relief, and instead find the path splits into two identical forks beyond it. The machine hums, unhelpful as ever, while you stand there turning your head between both paths, asking the trail itself, out loud, which way.
dochira.reading_mnemonic: You already know ど, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>どちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"doh-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no surprises left to decode.

doko.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's bag splits open and rice balls tumble everywhere. She scrambles after them, asking every passerby the same question over and over, all the way to the vending machine at the top: where did they go, where did that one land, where is the last one. The whole climb becomes one word, repeated: where.
doko.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>どこ</reading>, no hidden reading underneath.

donata.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hiker meets a stranger wrapped head to toe against the wind. Too winded to be casual, they bow deeply and ask with careful formality: might I ask, to whom do I have the honor of speaking? The mountain answers only with silence, and the polite question just hangs there: who, respectfully asked.
donata.reading_mnemonic: どなた is written exactly as it sounds, kana only — read straight through as <reading>どなた</reading>, no hidden reading to derive.
donata.description: This is the polite version of the plain word for who, used when asking after a stranger, a guest, or anyone you would address formally, the way English shifts from a blunt who's that to who, may I ask. Save the plain form for friends and family instead.

donna.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a clerk named Donna refuses to just ring anything up. She grabs every item — onigiri, drinks, gum — and interrogates the shopper: what kind of rice is inside, what kind of flavor, what kind of wrapper. The beeping till never moves on until she gets an answer to her only question: what kind of.
donna.reading_mnemonic: どんな is written exactly as it sounds — kana only, nothing to dig for — just read <reading>どんな</reading> straight through as it's written.

dono.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the onigiri shelf holds forty identical rice balls, and the man ahead of you has frozen solid, finger hovering back and forth while the till beeps behind him. Which one, which one, which one — he can never land on an answer, and now the whole line is stuck asking the same thing he is: which.
dono.reading_mnemonic: どの is written in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode — just sound out <reading>どの</reading> as it appears on the page.

dore.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school hallway has twelve identical doors, and behind exactly one of them a ball is bouncing. You work down the row knocking on every door, and each knock comes back the same hollow thud, so you start rattling handles instead. Twelve doors, one ball, and only one question left in your head — which one.
dore.reading_mnemonic: Written in kana just as it sounds, <reading>どれ</reading>, so there is nothing to work out.
dore.description: Asks you to pick from three or more things in view. When the choice is between exactly two, Japanese uses a different question word instead. Like its near and far partners, it stands alone as a pronoun and is not placed directly before a noun.

dou.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one impossible vending machine hums between the trees, accepting a coin no one on the trail carries. A hiker who just spent an hour climbing pokes button after button, turns to a stranger nearby, and asks the only sensible question left: how does this thing even work.
dou.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どう</reading>.

doushite.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and charges double for the same onigiri, for the third night running. Koichi stares at the receipt under the fluorescent lights, not with a customer's cool complaint but a genuine, immediate splutter — why, how come, what is going on here.
doushite.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どうして</reading>.
doushite.description: どうして carries more feeling than a neutral question — it often doubles as an exclamation of surprise or frustration, how did this even happen, rather than a calm request for a reason, and it's the version heard far more in casual conversation than in writing.

futatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The second raccoon inspects the snapped chopsticks on the table, short stick over long stick, and realizes they aren't cutlery anymore — just identical wooden splinters. It pockets both, satisfied that whatever it's counting tonight, the tally stops right there at <kanji>two</kanji> things, no broth-soaked evidence left to explain.
futatsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 二（ふた）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ふたつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
futatsu.description: Like its sibling word for one item, this is a native Japanese number used for counting generic objects on its own, without a separate counter word attached — distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counters for people, flat objects, and so on.

go-v.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same hooked hand reaches out from beside the vending machine, snagging snacks lined along the ledge. It's already got four stacked in your arms when the crooked hook swipes once more and lands a fifth off the top shelf. One hook, five snacks: that's the word for <kanji>five</kanji>.
go-v.reading_mnemonic: That practiced swipe already speaks the <reading>ご</reading> reading you learned for 五 — the clipped <reading>go</reading> you mutter to yourself right before you reach.

hachi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Those two strokes are still splitting wider at the bottom, the same spread that already meant <kanji>eight</kanji> when you met the kanji alone. Let that split happen four times over, fanned out beneath one twitching body, legs still moving until there are eight of them — a spider, standing on exactly the number this word names.
hachi-v.reading_mnemonic: This word borrows 八's own reading untouched, so it's read exactly <reading>はち</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji itself.

hitotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Backstage after her talent show, the goat is handed a raffle box to count the night's takings. She digs through it hoping for more, but there is exactly <kanji>one</kanji> ticket rattling around inside, no stub, no runner-up prize. She holds it to the light anyway, satisfied that at least one thing tonight was worth keeping.
hitotsu.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 一（ひと）plus the counter つ, giving you <reading>ひとつ</reading> exactly as you'd expect.
hitotsu.description: This is one of the native Japanese numbers used for counting generic objects, distinct from the Chinese-derived counting series paired with counter words for people, flat objects, and so on. It stands on its own without a separate counter attached, up through ten items.

hyaku-v.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane lights one stick of incense at the shrine, and the smoke catches the white glow off the mossy steps until it multiplies before her eyes, exactly like that lone stroke stacking over the whiteness. By the time she looks up, the courtyard cats have multiplied to match — a whole <kanji>hundred</kanji> of them prowling the steps.
hyaku-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 百 by itself, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>ひゃく</reading>.

ichi-v.meaning_mnemonic: Judging her own talent show yet again, the smug goat holds up a single hoof and announces the score before anyone can ask: <kanji>one</kanji> out of one. There was only ever one entrant, one stage, one strip of dirt to stand on, so the number was settled before the show even began. She says it like a verdict, not a count: one.
ichi-v.reading_mnemonic: One line, one reading: 一 alone still reads <reading>いち</reading>, the same reading you already learned for it standing by itself.

ikaga.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat dragging a rice offering off the shrine's mossy steps. Instead of shouting, she bows a fraction and asks, syrupy with formality, how the day has been treating it. The cat freezes mid-theft, offering still in its mouth, trapped by the world's politest how. Courtesy, not curiosity, is the whole word.
ikaga.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いかが</reading>」.

ikura.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself up the mountain trail to the vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting water. The display keeps climbing past every price he's paid for a drink, digit by digit, as he jabs the button asking how much this could possibly cost. It never stops long enough to answer — the only punchline the machine needs.
ikura.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくら</reading>」.
ikura.description: いくら written this way is also the everyday word for salmon roe, the bright orange fish eggs served over rice — a completely different word that happens to share the same sound and spelling. Context sorts them out fast: paired with a price or a question, it means how much; sitting on a plate, it means the food.

ikutsu.meaning_mnemonic: A kid parked at Koichi's till points at the leaning tower of onigiri and demands how many are stacked there. Koichi starts counting, and halfway through, the kid swivels and asks the identical question about his age. The tower wobbles, forgotten, as Koichi answers both with the same flat number — how many and how old are one demand wearing two coats to this kid.
ikutsu.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくつ</reading>」.

ima.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat ducks under the eaves the instant the rain starts — exactly the <kanji>now</kanji> image, a person taking cover under a wide roof, caring about nothing before or after. It won't budge from that dry spot even when the enormous bell rings, because for that cat there is no later, only this exact drip-free moment: now.
ima.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 今 read with the kun'yomi you already know, standing alone as 「<reading>いま</reading>」.

itsu.meaning_mnemonic: A heron standing in the shallows at the riverbank wears a wristwatch and answers questions for free. You ask about the water going down: it's two. You ask about the ferry: it's two. You ask about getting your own watch back off its leg: it's two. Ask a heron anything and it hands you a time, so the question you are really asking is when.
itsu.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, so <reading>いつ</reading> is both the spelling and the reading — nothing to decode.
itsu.description: English lets you say when for both the question and the joining word, as in the sentence about what happens when it rains. This word only does the question. The joining sense uses different grammar entirely.

itsutsu.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, your arm still cramped into the hooked shape from the character for <kanji>five</kanji> reaching sideways. Coins drop, cans thunk out one after another, and on the fifth thunk your hooked hand snags it before it hits the dirt. Five cans lined up at your feet, caught in one long, aching reach: five things.
itsutsu.reading_mnemonic: 五 already carries the reading <reading>いつ</reading>, and つ stays つ, giving you exactly <reading>いつつ</reading> — five things, straight from the readings you already know.

juu-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps once for every raised finger, and the cashier keeps raising both hands until every finger is up, tracing the same <kanji>ten</kanji> cross in the air. The till stops beeping exactly when both hands are full — ten, and not one beep more.
juu-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 十 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>じゅう</reading>.

kanojo.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi points across the konbini at the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> restocking the onigiri shelf, arm sweeping the row into place. He doesn't explain, just tilts his head and grins: that's the one he's been talking about all week. You don't need more than that look to know she's his girlfriend, and now you know who she is too.
kanojo.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, she keeps introducing the same woman standing by the bell alongside a man named Joe: Kane, and Joe. Say it fast — <reading>Kane-Joe</reading> — and you land on <reading>かのじょ</reading>, the word for her, the girlfriend everyone at the shrine already knows by name.

kare.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron keeps prying the side mirror off a toy car and dropping it at the feet of whichever man happens to be standing closest, like a tiny crown. The locals start calling that unlucky guy by the same word every single time — and since he's always some woman's boyfriend waiting there for her, the word settles on him: he, boyfriend.
kare.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron drops a plastic toy <reading>car</reading> at your feet, and someone mutters <reading>かれ</reading>, eh, nodding toward whichever man it landed nearest — and the name sticks to him alone, every single time the bird does it.

kimi.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the coach's whistle breaks, so instead of names he just barks the same word at whichever kid is nearest the ball — kimi, kimi — pointing, never naming. By the end of practice the whole team answers to it, the casual, jabbing word you'd only ever aim at a friend or someone younger than you.
kimi.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a scruffy stray dog answers only to the coach's shout of <reading>きみ</reading> — it sounds just like calling out <reading>key, me!</reading> while he jangles his whistle-keys — and the dog comes running to whichever kid the coach is jabbing a finger at.

kochira.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, on the sports field, the coach spots a shy transfer student hovering by the gate and waves the whole team over with one arm: this way, everyone — then, turning to the team, this is our new player. One gesture does both jobs, aiming a direction and introducing a person, which is exactly what this word covers: this way, this person.
kochira.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it's read — <reading>こちら</reading>, nothing to derive.
kochira.description: This is the polite register: it is what you use to gesture someone toward a direction in front of others, or to introduce a person formally (a host presenting a guest, a clerk directing a customer), not casual chatter between friends about where something is.

koko.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane rings the shrine's one enormous bell every morning, but the rope has vanished among the mossy steps and circling cats. She stamps one paving stone and declares the rope must be tied down right there, jabbing the ground: here, here, here — and that exact stamped spot is where it's always been.
koko.reading_mnemonic: ここ is pure kana, read exactly as it looks, so there's no hidden kanji to unpack — <reading>ここ</reading> is simply pronounced as written.

kokonotsu.meaning_mnemonic: Hana reaches switchback <kanji>nine</kanji> on the mountain trail, exactly where hikers lean their hooked canes against the rock to catch their breath. Someone already got there first — not one cane but a whole row of them, hooked over the same ledge like abandoned question marks. She counts twice to be sure: nine things, propped together at the ninth bend.
kokonotsu.reading_mnemonic: This word simply takes 九's kun'yomi reading ここの and adds つ, the counter for physical things, giving 「<reading>ここのつ</reading>」.

konna.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi is standing behind his own register, holding up the onigiri that is already in his hand, insisting to the customer that no substitute will do — only this kind of rice ball, the exact one gripped between his fingers, right here and nowhere else.
konna.reading_mnemonic: This word is written the way it sounds, straight kana, so <reading>こんな</reading> is read exactly as it looks — no hidden reading to hunt for.

kono.meaning_mnemonic: You are in Koichi's konbini holding a waffle cone, and the beeping till will not stop until you name what you are buying. You do not know the word for cone, so you jab it at Koichi and repeat cone-oh, cone-oh until he gives up. He rings up whatever you are jabbing at: this cone, this onigiri, this rice ball — always the one right here in your hand.
kono.reading_mnemonic: There is nothing to decode here: the word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>この</reading>.
kono.description: Always attaches directly to a noun and never stands on its own. English happily says I want this with nothing after it; this word cannot do that, and a bare this needs a different standalone word. It marks the thing as near you, the speaker, rather than near the person you are talking to.

kore.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you jab a finger at the onigiri closest to you, ignoring the whole shelf behind it. The cashier doesn't ask which one — pointing already decided it. That's the one you meant, this one, and nothing else on the shelf matters anymore.
kore.reading_mnemonic: これ is kana all the way through, no kanji hiding underneath — just read <reading>これ</reading> exactly the way it's written.

ku-num.meaning_mnemonic: That same hook is on closing duty tonight, yanking down the shutter at Koichi's konbini one slat at a time. It catches, drags, catches again — nine short tugs before the shutter seals shut, and the last tug is the one that lands on <kanji>nine</kanji>, alt reading and all, right as the beeping till goes quiet.
ku-num.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lone dove has nested in among the cats, and none of them touch it. When the bell rings, it doesn't screech — it lets out one flat <reading>coo</reading>, over and over, and that flat sound is exactly how this word is read: <reading>く</reading>.

kyuu-v.meaning_mnemonic: The hook is still propped at the last switchback of the mountain trail, right where you left it leaning into <kanji>nine</kanji>. This time it's snagged a sock, blown off a line at the riverbank and dragged all the way up, caught fast on the hook at the top — bend nine, the last one, the whole climb done.
kyuu-v.reading_mnemonic: This word just keeps 九's own reading, so it's read exactly <reading>きゅう</reading>, the same sound you already learned for the kanji by itself.

man-v.meaning_mnemonic: Someone climbs a ladder to recount the banner's zeros herself, licking a finger to peel back each heavy fold of cloth. Her arms give out before the counting does, so she chalks a final total on the last scrap of space and declares the stall sold out at <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> onigiri — not one more, not one less.
man-v.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just 万 read <reading>まん</reading>, exactly like the banner kanji you already know.
man-v.description: Japanese counts large numbers in blocks of ten thousand rather than thousands, so 万 anchors the whole system used for big figures. English commas group by thousands, so converting between the two takes practice — a million lands on a multiple of ten thousand here, not on a clean round number.

mittsu.meaning_mnemonic: You're at the riverbank stacking flat stones into a cairn, the way the character for <kanji>three</kanji> stacks its own three flat lines. One stone, then a second balanced on top, and just as the tower wobbles you set down a third to steady it. Three stones, standing exactly as tall as the character taught you: three things, balanced and done.
mittsu.reading_mnemonic: 三 already carries the reading <reading>みっ</reading>, and つ stays つ, so together they give you exactly <reading>みっつ</reading> — three things, built straight from readings you already know.

muttsu.meaning_mnemonic: The lid clamps down on eight again, this time capping a stack of teacups on the shrine steps outside Grandma Kane's hall. Two cups vanish under the pressure, same trick as always, and the cats scatter as the stack settles low. She counts what is left before ringing the bell: <kanji>six</kanji> teacups, six things, capped for good.
muttsu.reading_mnemonic: 六 reads むっ here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>むっつ</reading>」.

nan.meaning_mnemonic: Cats keep arriving on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and you gave up asking what a cat is hours ago. Every question you have left comes with a number stuck to it: how many cats, what floor they have reached, what time they stop. This is the shape the question takes when a counter follows — what, before counters.
nan.reading_mnemonic: A tiny <reading>nun</reading> has claimed the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and runs it like a ticket window. She will not press a button until you say <reading>なん</reading> and then the counter for what you want, and she makes you start again if you mumble the number.
nan.description: This is the same word as the standalone question, wearing the shape it takes when a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows it. You almost never meet it alone; it arrives glued to whatever is being counted.

nana-v.meaning_mnemonic: By the door of Koichi's konbini, the coat hook is really just one bent nail sticking out of the wall. A delivery driver piles dripping rain jackets onto it between beeps of the till, one after another, until the nail bends almost flat under the weight. You count the jackets before it snaps: <kanji>seven</kanji>, all hanging off one crooked hook.
nana-v.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here is the one you already know from the kanji itself: <reading>なな</reading>.

nanatsu.meaning_mnemonic: The hook by the konbini door already sags under a full row of <kanji>seven</kanji> coats, bent halfway into the wall from the weight. A customer tries to squeeze one more sleeve onto it and the whole thing groans, but the hook holds firm — it was built to carry exactly seven things and not one more.
nanatsu.reading_mnemonic: 七 reads なな here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>ななつ</reading>」.

nani.meaning_mnemonic: A frazzled nanny in the echoing hallways of Sei's school is handed things by a toddler all morning: a wet sock, half a stapler, a beetle that is still alive. She has stopped guessing what any of it is. She just holds each object out at arm's length and asks the one flat question that covers all of it — what.
nani.reading_mnemonic: The same <reading>nanny</reading> takes a night shift at Koichi's konbini, and every time the beeping till coughs up an item she does not recognise she holds it over the onigiri shelf and says <reading>なに</reading> at the ceiling. By closing she has said it forty times and solved nothing.
nani.description: On its own — as a bare question, or with most particles — the word takes this reading. When a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows, it switches to the shorter reading you learn separately.

nannji.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the <kanji>time</kanji>-sun still crawls its slow arc overhead. A dazed tourist wanders in, squinting up, unable to read a single hour off it, and grabs a passing cat to blurt the same question over and over: what <kanji>time</kanji> is it? Her whole visit is just that one question: what time.
nannji.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, a jetlagged traveler keeps calling to her grandmother, 'Nan, gee, what time is it?' — sliding into <reading>Nan-gee</reading> each time. The cats now answer back with that same sound, <reading>なんじ</reading>, since that's all anyone there asks: what time.

naze.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line for the ninth time and finds nothing but a waterlogged boot, same as the last eight. He doesn't swear, doesn't sigh — he just plants his feet in the mud, glares at the current, and asks the only question left standing: why.
naze.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>なぜ</reading>.
naze.description: なぜ reads as blunter and more formal than a casual why — common in writing, official questions, and pointed interrogation. Dropped into an ordinary chat with a friend, on its own it can land as accusatory rather than merely curious.

ni-v.meaning_mnemonic: The waiter arrives to ask how many are dining and finds his answer already snapped in half on the table: two chopsticks, a short one laid over a long one, matching exactly like the pair of raccoons who broke them that way. He doesn't need to count paws underneath — the <kanji>two</kanji> sticks already told him. Table for two.
ni-v.reading_mnemonic: 二 alone already reads <reading>に</reading>, the same reading it carried in the chopstick story — nothing new to learn here.

rei.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a ranger posts an official notice board each morning with the exact temperature. One frost-bitten dawn, the mercury refuses to rise past the middle line at all, and the ranger stamps the report with one stiff, formal number before trudging back down. That number is zero.
rei.reading_mnemonic: The ranger reading the thermometer is named Ray, and he announces temperatures stiffly, formally, no contractions ever. He reads the number in one clipped word, <reading>れい</reading> — <reading>Ray</reading> only sounds this formal when the mercury freezes at zero.
rei.description: 零 is the formal, written register for zero — the word you'd see on an official temperature report or hear in a stiff announcement, not the one you'd use casually reading out a phone number or a game score.

roku-v.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, eight cats are sprawled across the mossy steps at dawn. She sets the heavy iron offering lid down with a clang right on the top step, and two cats bolt at the sound, tails high. What's left staring up at the enormous bell is <kanji>six</kanji> cats, thoroughly unimpressed by the racket. The lid on top of eight, as always, leaves <kanji>six</kanji>.
roku-v.reading_mnemonic: 六's reading here is just the number's own reading you already learned: <reading>ろく</reading>.

san-v.meaning_mnemonic: A teacher taps a chalk pointer against three stacked lines on the board, one, two, three, and by the third tap the class already knows what word is coming before she says it. There is no trick to uncover here: <kanji>three</kanji> lines stacked in a character just spells the word three, plainly, the way it has all along.
san-v.reading_mnemonic: 三 alone already reads <reading>さん</reading>, the same reading you counted out tapping the three lines.

sen-v.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine's price display multiplies without warning: one bold slash scratches straight across the readout, the same slash that once capped that plus-sign cross into something bigger, and the number keeps climbing past every digit until it locks on one round <kanji>thousand</kanji> and finally stops beeping.
sen-v.reading_mnemonic: This word is just the kanji 千 on its own, so it keeps exactly the reading you already know: <reading>せん</reading>.

shi-num.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the same sealed box waits among the mossy steps, its trapped mouth still murmuring numbers into the corner. A cat swats it off the step and the lid cracks — the mouth peeks out just far enough to hiss a hushed <kanji>four</kanji> before a monk claps the lid shut, refusing to let it say the number again.
shi-num.reading_mnemonic: That hushed <reading>し</reading> is the same reading 四 already taught you — the clipped <reading>shh</reading> the monk uses to cut the mouth off mid-count.
shi-num.description: This reading of 四 sounds identical to a much darker word, so hospitals, hotels, and gift-givers avoid it — floor numbers, room numbers, and counted items switch to the other reading, よん, instead. Learn to recognize both, but default to よん when you're the one speaking.

shichi-num.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, the same bent-nail hook holds gym jerseys instead of coats. There's only one hook by the lockers, so seven players fresh off the field cram their jerseys onto it at once, the nail sagging nearly sideways under the pile. The coach counts before it gives way: <kanji>seven</kanji> jerseys, all balanced on one crooked hook.
shichi-num.reading_mnemonic: 七's reading here keeps the reading you already learned for formal counting: <reading>しち</reading>.
shichi-num.description: しち is the older, more formal reading of 七 — used in compounds, in reading dates and times aloud, and in fixed set phrases. なな is generally preferred when counting items alone or aloud, since しち can be mistaken for the word for one in quick speech.

sochira.meaning_mnemonic: You're already at Koichi's till, practically leaning on the register, when you ask where the onigiri is. Koichi doesn't even look up — he just tilts his chin two feet toward the shelf you're basically touching and grunts the sound out, because when the thing you want is that close, all you need to say is that way.
sochira.reading_mnemonic: You already know そ, ち, and ら from other kana words; <reading>そちら</reading> just strings them together into the sound <reading>"so-chee-rah"</reading>, read exactly as it's spelled, no twist to catch you out.

soko.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone drops a sandal mid-crossing and it snags on a rock partway across the water. You point at the exact spot from the near bank, arm out straight, calling out to the person wading in: there, there, no, THERE — the sandal never moves, but your pointing finger fixes the place for good.
soko.reading_mnemonic: そこ is written entirely in kana the way it sounds, with no kanji standing behind it — you read <reading>そこ</reading> exactly as it's spelled.

sonna.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat knocks the enormous bell clean off its stand, and when she's told it was an accident she just stares at the wreckage — that kind of excuse, the kind aimed right back at whoever just spoke, never quite convincing her.
sonna.reading_mnemonic: Like its cousins, this word is pure kana, so <reading>そんな</reading> is pronounced exactly as spelled, with nothing underneath to decode.

sono.meaning_mnemonic: Your friend is squatting on the riverbank with three soaked shoes lined up beside them, and you are holding a sonar gun that refuses to lock onto anything near you. It only pings at objects sitting next to somebody else, whining so-no, so-no as it swings toward them. Whatever it picks out is that shoe, that bucket, that dripping thing over by your friend.
sono.reading_mnemonic: No decoding needed: this word is spelled in kana precisely as it is pronounced, <reading>その</reading>.
sono.description: Attaches directly to a noun and never stands alone. It points at something in the listener's zone rather than yours, so a thing in their hand or on their side of the table takes this word even where English would say this. It also picks up something the other person has just mentioned, with nothing visible to point at.

sore.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini a customer holds an onigiri up under your nose, and your pointing finger is so sore from a full shift at the beeping till that you can barely straighten it. You waggle the sore finger at the rice ball sitting there in his hands and grunt. Whatever is over by him, close enough for him to touch — that one.
sore.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, <reading>それ</reading>, so there is no reading to decode.
sore.description: Points at something near the person you are talking to, rather than near you — the middle rung of the near, middle, far set. It stands alone as a pronoun, so it never sits directly in front of a noun; the form that does that is a separate word.

too.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, someone has arranged the onigiri into a stack of perfect crosses — the <kanji>ten</kanji> mark hikers make with two raised hands when they reach a full count. There are ten of them lined up by the register, each shaped like that same cross, and the till beeps once for every single one as the clerk recounts them. Ten things, stacked in crosses at the counter.
too.reading_mnemonic: This word is just 十's kun'yomi reading standing alone as the number word for ten things: 「<reading>とお</reading>」.

watashi.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tanuki knocks over the shiny new security mirror by the till and freezes, nose to nose with itself. It taps the glass, tilts its head, and decides, flatly, that the animal staring back must be the most important customer in the store: itself. From then on it restocks the onigiri shelf for nobody else, certain of exactly who it means when it talks about I.
watashi.reading_mnemonic: The tanuki taps the glass and gasps at what it sees — <reading>what a shiny</reading> creature — then realizes it's only its own reflection, saying <reading>わたし</reading>, I, over and over, delighted that the shiniest thing in the konbini turned out to be itself.

watashitachi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat rings the enormous bell and every other cat in the place mobs the sound, wedging in shoulder to shoulder until they're one solid, purring mass on the step. Ask any single cat its name and the whole pile answers at once, because as far as they're concerned there's no such thing as one cat here anymore, only the pile. That fused, shoulder-to-shoulder answer is the meaning you want: we.
watashitachi.reading_mnemonic: Try to pet just one cat in the pile and the whole mass yowls back what sounds like <reading>what a she, touchy</reading> bunch — really the cats shouting <reading>わたしたち</reading>, we, in one voice, refusing to be split apart even for the bell.

yattsu.meaning_mnemonic: At the base of the mountain trail, two hikers' legs split wider with every step up the steep slope, spreading apart like the shape of the number <kanji>eight</kanji> itself. By the vending machine at the top, you count the pairs of boots left behind by exhausted climbers: eight things, scattered where the trail finally levels out.
yattsu.reading_mnemonic: 八 reads やっ here and combines with the counter つ, giving you 「<reading>やっつ</reading>」.

yon-v.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till at Koichi's konbini sits that same sealed box, the mouth still trapped inside counting onigiri through the glass. Tonight it's a slow delivery — one, two, three — and on the next rice ball the mouth presses flat against the glass and stops. That flattened stare is the number stamped on this word: <kanji>four</kanji>.
yon-v.reading_mnemonic: Nothing to derive here — 四 already taught you the <reading>よん</reading> reading, the same stretch you reach for right before a big <reading>yawn</reading>.

yottsu.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the trapped <kanji>four</kanji> mouth from inside the enclosure has escaped into the stockroom and wedged itself into a cardboard case behind the counter, still muttering its count under its breath. Koichi hauls the case onto the shelf and counts what's rattling around inside: four onigiri, no more, no less. Four things, sealed in one box.
yottsu.reading_mnemonic: 四 already carries the reading <reading>よっ</reading>, and つ stays つ, giving you exactly <reading>よっつ</reading> — four things, straight from readings you already know.

zero.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team spends the entire match slipping on the wet grass, missing every shot, while the goalkeeper falls asleep against the post. The final whistle blows, the scoreboard locks in one flat, humiliating number, and the whole bench stares at it in silence. That number is zero.
zero.reading_mnemonic: ゼロ is spelled exactly the way it sounds — read the katakana <reading>ゼロ</reading> straight through, no hidden reading to dig for.
zero.description: ゼロ is the everyday spoken form, heard in scores, phone numbers, and casual temperature talk; formal or written contexts often reach for a different, more formal word instead.
